title: Eggs for a Hangover: Do They Help? The Cysteine Science, Explained
excerpt: Are eggs good for a hangover? What the cysteine in eggs does with acetaldehyde, how much a serving really provides, the best ways to eat them, and the raw-egg myth.
metaDescription: Are eggs good for a hangover? How the cysteine in eggs relates to acetaldehyde, how much you really get, the best ways to eat them, and what to skip.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** eggs are one of the better things you can eat the morning after drinking, but not because they "cure" a hangover. They're easy on a queasy stomach, they bring protein and a little fat that steady your blood sugar, and they contain cysteine, an amino acid your body uses to help clear acetaldehyde (a toxic by-product of alcohol) and to rebuild glutathione, one of your liver's main antioxidants. That cysteine link is real chemistry, but the amount in a couple of eggs is modest, and there is no good evidence from human trials that eating eggs makes a hangover shorter or milder. Think of eggs as a smart, gentle breakfast that helps you recover, not as a treatment.

**The quick version for this morning:** have one to three eggs, cooked the way your stomach can handle (soft scrambled or boiled are the gentlest), with a slice of toast or some fruit, plus a big glass of water or an electrolyte drink. Skip raw eggs in "hangover cocktails." If you can't keep anything down, start with fluids and plain carbs and add the eggs later.

> **When to see a doctor.** A normal hangover is miserable but passes within a day. Get medical help if you or someone else **can't stop vomiting or can't keep fluids down for several hours**, **vomits blood or something that looks like coffee grounds**, has **severe stomach pain**, is **confused, very drowsy, or hard to wake**, has **a seizure**, or has **slow or irregular breathing**. These can be signs of alcohol poisoning, severe dehydration, or another emergency, so call 911 (or your local emergency number). Shaking, sweating, racing heart, or seeing or hearing things after cutting back on regular heavy drinking can be signs of alcohol withdrawal, which can be dangerous and needs medical care, not breakfast. This article is general information, not medical advice.

## Why Eggs Show Up on Every Hangover List

Search for hangover foods and eggs appear almost everywhere, from diner breakfasts to the bacon, egg, and cheese sandwich that's practically a New York institution. Part of that is habit: eggs are cheap, fast, and already in the fridge. But there are three real reasons they make sense after a night out.

1. **They contain cysteine.** This sulfur-containing amino acid is the part of the story most articles focus on, and it has a genuine connection to how your body handles alcohol. More on this below.
2. **They're gentle and filling.** A hangover often comes with nausea and a stomach that doesn't want anything greasy or acidic. Eggs are soft, mild, and give you protein without much bulk.
3. **They help steady your energy.** Drinking can disrupt blood sugar control, and some people feel shaky and weak the next morning. A breakfast that pairs protein and fat with some carbohydrate releases energy more evenly than a sugary snack alone.

None of those make eggs special in a magical sense. They make eggs a sensible choice. That distinction matters, because the internet tends to turn "sensible" into "guaranteed fix."

## The Cysteine Connection, Explained in Plain Words

To understand why eggs get linked to hangovers, it helps to know what your body does with alcohol.

### Step 1: Alcohol becomes acetaldehyde

When you drink, your liver breaks alcohol (ethanol) down in two main steps. First, an enzyme called alcohol dehydrogenase turns ethanol into **acetaldehyde**. Acetaldehyde is the nasty one. It's toxic, it's reactive, and researchers believe it contributes to some hangover symptoms such as nausea, flushing, a racing heart, and headache, though it's only one piece of a bigger picture.

### Step 2: Acetaldehyde becomes acetate

A second enzyme, aldehyde dehydrogenase, turns acetaldehyde into acetate, which is relatively harmless and eventually becomes carbon dioxide and water. When you drink faster than your liver can keep up, acetaldehyde can build up in the meantime.

### Where cysteine fits in

Cysteine has a sulfur group that can react directly with acetaldehyde and bind it into a more stable compound. Lab and animal research going back to the 1970s showed that giving cysteine could protect rats from otherwise harmful doses of acetaldehyde. That's the original reason people got interested in cysteine as a hangover aid.

Cysteine also matters for a second reason. It's one of the three building blocks of **glutathione**, an antioxidant your liver uses to neutralize reactive by-products, including some generated when alcohol is processed. Of the three building blocks, cysteine is usually the one in shortest supply, so it tends to set the pace for how fast your body can make more glutathione. Our guide to [glutathione for hangovers](/never-hungover/glutathione-for-hangover) goes deeper on that side of the story.

### Do eggs actually give you enough?

This is where the story gets more honest than most articles. Eggs do contain cysteine, but not a huge amount. Based on USDA nutrient data, a large egg provides very roughly 130 to 150 mg of cysteine. Two eggs gives you something like 250 to 300 mg.

The best-known human study on cysteine and hangovers, a small randomized, placebo-controlled trial from Finland published in *Alcohol and Alcoholism* in 2020, used a supplement containing **1,200 mg of L-cysteine** along with some vitamins. The researchers reported less nausea and headache in some measures, and less stress and anxiety the next day, in a group of fewer than 20 young men. It was a small study, it tested a concentrated supplement rather than food, and it hasn't been widely repeated. It's interesting, not settled.

So the realistic takeaway is:

- The idea behind eggs and cysteine is grounded in real chemistry.
- A normal serving of eggs delivers a fraction of the dose used in that trial.
- Your body also digests the protein in eggs slowly and spreads the cysteine through the day, rather than delivering one concentrated hit.
- There is no good evidence from human trials that eating eggs, specifically, reduces hangover symptoms.

If you want the full picture on cysteine as a supplement, including doses and the limits of that research, see our [L-cysteine for hangover guide](/never-hungover/l-cysteine-for-hangover).

## Other Things Eggs Bring to the Table

Cysteine gets the headlines, but eggs have a few other qualities that are useful the morning after.

### Protein that's easy to digest

A large egg has about 6 grams of high-quality protein. Protein helps you feel full, slows the rise and fall of blood sugar when eaten with carbohydrates, and is generally easier on a sensitive stomach than heavy, fried foods.

### Choline and B vitamins

Eggs are one of the richest common sources of **choline**, a nutrient the liver uses to package and move fat. They also provide vitamin B12, riboflavin (B2), and some folate. Heavy drinking over time is associated with lower levels of several B vitamins, and a single night out won't drain you, but a nutrient-dense breakfast is a better reset than an empty stomach or a pastry. To be clear, there's no evidence that the choline or B vitamins in a couple of eggs will noticeably change how a hangover feels.

### A little fat, not a lot

A large egg has around 5 grams of fat. That's enough to make a meal satisfying without the heavy, greasy load of a full fry-up, which some people find makes their nausea worse.

### Mild flavor and texture

This sounds trivial, but it's one of the most practical reasons. When you're nauseated, strong smells, sharp acidity, and heavy textures can push you over the edge. Soft scrambled eggs are about as inoffensive as food gets.

## The Bigger Reasons You Feel Bad (and What Eggs Can and Can't Fix)

A hangover isn't one problem. Researchers who study hangovers describe it as a mix of several things happening at once. Knowing which is which helps you set realistic expectations for any food.

| What's going on | What it feels like | Do eggs help? |
|---|---|---|
| Acetaldehyde and other by-products | Nausea, headache, feeling "poisoned" | A little, in theory, via cysteine. The dose in food is small. |
| Dehydration and lost electrolytes | Thirst, dry mouth, headache, dizziness | No. You need fluids and electrolytes. |
| Low or unstable blood sugar | Shakiness, weakness, irritability, poor focus | Yes, when eaten with some carbohydrate. |
| Irritated stomach lining | Nausea, stomach pain, poor appetite | Eggs are gentle, which helps you eat at all. |
| Poor-quality sleep | Fatigue, brain fog | No. Only rest fixes this. |
| Inflammation from the immune system | General achiness, feeling unwell | No direct evidence. |
| Congeners (extra compounds in dark drinks) | Often worse hangovers after whiskey, red wine, brandy | No. |

The honest summary: eggs mainly help with the "I need to eat something that won't make me feel worse" problem and the blood-sugar problem. Everything else still needs time, fluids, and rest.

## How to Eat Eggs for a Hangover

### The best ways to cook them when you feel rough

- **Soft scrambled eggs.** The easiest on the stomach. Cook them low and slow with a small knob of butter or a splash of milk. Avoid loading them with hot sauce if you're nauseated.
- **Boiled eggs.** No fat added, easy to make while you're half awake, and easy to eat in small bites. Good if your stomach is very unsettled.
- **Poached eggs on toast.** Toast adds the plain carbohydrate that helps your blood sugar, and it soaks up yolk so the whole thing goes down easily.
- **An omelet with spinach or tomato.** Good once you're feeling a bit better and want more substance and some vegetables.
- **Egg drop soup or a brothy egg soup.** Salty broth helps replace sodium and fluid, and the egg adds protein. Many cultures have a version of this, from Chinese egg drop soup to Italian stracciatella.

### What to pair them with

Eggs are a component, not a whole recovery plan. Round them out with:

- **Plain carbohydrate:** toast, a bagel, rice, or oatmeal to bring your blood sugar back up.
- **Fruit:** a banana adds potassium, and berries or orange slices add some vitamin C and fluid.
- **Fluids:** water first, and an electrolyte drink if you were sweating, vomiting, or drank a lot. Our guide to [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) explains when they actually help.
- **Salt in moderation:** a pinch on your eggs isn't a bad thing after a night when you lost fluids.

### How many eggs?

One to three is a normal serving for most adults. There's no benefit to forcing down six eggs to "get more cysteine." You won't come anywhere close to supplement-level doses, and overeating on a sensitive stomach is a quick route to feeling worse.

### Timing

If you can eat as soon as you wake up, great. If you can't face food yet, sip water or a sports drink, wait 30 to 60 minutes, then try something plain like dry toast. Eggs can come next once your stomach settles. Our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) has more on easing back into eating.

## The Bacon, Egg, and Cheese Question

The breakfast sandwich is many people's hangover ritual, and plenty of search interest is about exactly this. Is a greasy egg sandwich good for a hangover?

It depends on your stomach. Here's the honest trade-off:

- **What it does well:** it combines protein (egg), carbohydrate (bread), fat, and salt, which together can make you feel more human, especially if you skipped dinner. The salt helps a little with fluid balance, and it's satisfying.
- **Where it can backfire:** a lot of grease can slow down how fast your stomach empties, which some people experience as heavier nausea or reflux, especially if alcohol has already irritated the stomach lining. Processed meats are also high in salt and fat, which isn't ideal as a regular habit.

There's no evidence that greasy food "soaks up" alcohol the next morning. By the time you're hungover, the alcohol has already been absorbed and mostly processed. A fatty meal is more useful *before* or *while* you drink, when it slows how quickly alcohol reaches your bloodstream. Our guide on [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide) covers that side.

If a bacon, egg, and cheese sounds good and your stomach agrees, enjoy it. If you're queasy, a lighter version (egg and cheese on toast, or a boiled egg and a banana) is usually the better call.

## Raw Eggs and the "Prairie Oyster"

There's an old hangover "cure" called the **prairie oyster**: a raw egg yolk swallowed whole with Worcestershire sauce, hot sauce, salt, and pepper, sometimes with a splash of vinegar or tomato juice. It turns up in old bartending books and in films, and it has a theatrical, kill-or-cure reputation.

There is no good evidence that it works any better than cooked eggs. It also carries a real downside: raw eggs can carry *Salmonella*, a bacterium that causes food poisoning. Food safety agencies such as the US FDA and CDC advise against eating raw or undercooked eggs, especially for pregnant people, young children, older adults, and anyone with a weakened immune system. The last thing a dehydrated, nauseated person needs is a bout of vomiting and diarrhea on top.

If you love the ritual, pasteurized eggs reduce the risk. But a cooked egg gives you the same nutrients and the same cysteine without the gamble.

## Eggs Versus Other Popular Hangover Foods

Eggs aren't the only food with a hangover reputation. Here's how they compare with other common choices, judged on what each actually offers.

| Food | Main benefit after drinking | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| **Eggs** | Gentle protein, some cysteine, steady energy | Raw eggs; very greasy preparations |
| **Toast or crackers** | Plain carbs, easy on nausea | Not much else nutritionally |
| **Bananas** | Potassium, easy carbs | Not a fix for dehydration on its own |
| **Broth or soup** | Fluid and sodium | Very salty instant versions |
| **Oatmeal** | Slow-release carbs, gentle | Can feel heavy for some |
| **Watermelon or fruit** | Fluid and natural sugar | Acidic fruit can bother an upset stomach |
| **Greasy fry-up** | Satisfying, salty | Can worsen nausea and reflux |
| **Coffee** | Alertness | Can irritate the stomach and doesn't rehydrate you well |

The common thread: good hangover food is gentle, provides some carbohydrate and fluid, and doesn't overwhelm a sensitive stomach. Eggs fit that profile well, which is why they deserve their place on the list. For a wider look at what helps and what doesn't, our [complete hangover science guide](/never-hungover/how-to-cure-a-hangover-complete-science-guide) walks through the evidence for each approach.

## Common Myths About Eggs and Hangovers

**Myth: Eggs "absorb" or "neutralize" the alcohol in your system.**
By morning, alcohol has already been absorbed. Eggs can't pull it back out. The cysteine in them can play a small role in clearing acetaldehyde, but that's a modest biochemical contribution, not a sponge.

**Myth: More eggs means a faster recovery.**
There's no evidence for a dose-response effect from eating more eggs. A normal serving is enough to get the practical benefits (protein, steady energy, something gentle to eat).

**Myth: Egg whites alone are better because they're "cleaner."**
The yolk carries most of the choline, B vitamins, and fat, and some of the flavor that makes eggs easier to eat when you're struggling. Whole eggs are a perfectly good choice unless your doctor has told you otherwise.

**Myth: Eggs before bed will stop tomorrow's hangover.**
A late-night snack may help a little if you didn't eat dinner, mainly by giving your body some fuel. It won't undo heavy drinking. What matters most is how much you drank and how fast.

## Should You Take a Cysteine Supplement Instead?

Some people read about cysteine and wonder whether a pill would work better than breakfast. A few points to keep in mind:

- **The human evidence is limited.** The main trial was small, and results like these need to be repeated in larger, independent studies before anyone can say much with confidence.
- **N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is a related but different compound.** It's a form of cysteine used in hospitals as the antidote for acetaminophen (Tylenol) overdose. As a daily supplement, the evidence for hangovers is thin. If you take medications, check with a pharmacist or doctor before adding NAC. Our [NAC vs DHM comparison](/never-hungover/nac-vs-dhm-which-antioxidant-better-liver-protection-2025) lays out the differences.
- **Supplements are not a license to drink more.** No pill or food changes the basic math: the more you drink, the worse you're likely to feel.

For most people, eggs are a good food choice and a cysteine supplement is an optional experiment, not a necessity.

## Who Should Be Careful With Eggs

Eggs are safe for most people, but a few groups should take note:

- **People with an egg allergy**, which is one of the more common food allergies, especially in children.
- **People whose doctor has advised them to limit dietary cholesterol** because of heart disease or diabetes. Current dietary guidance is more relaxed about eggs than it once was, but your own doctor's advice comes first.
- **Pregnant people, older adults, and anyone with a weakened immune system**, who should avoid raw or runny eggs because of the food-poisoning risk.

## A Smarter Morning: The Full Recovery Routine

Eggs are one helpful piece. Here's a simple, evidence-led routine for the morning after a night out:

1. **Rehydrate first.** A large glass of water as soon as you're up, then keep sipping. Add an electrolyte drink if you vomited or drank a lot.
2. **Eat something gentle within an hour or two.** Eggs on toast with a banana is a solid default.
3. **Treat the headache carefully if you need to.** If you reach for a painkiller, follow the label, take it with food, and be careful with acetaminophen if you drink heavily. Our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains the risks.
4. **Rest.** Sleep after drinking is often poor quality. A nap or an early night helps more than any food.
5. **Go easy on caffeine.** A cup of coffee is fine if you're used to it, but don't rely on it to rehydrate you.
6. **Plan for next time.** Eating a real meal before drinking, alternating alcoholic drinks with water, and drinking less overall do far more than anything you eat the next day. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best support.

## Where DHM Fits In

If you're reading about cysteine because you're interested in how the body processes alcohol, you've probably also come across **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree. Like the cysteine story, the DHM story is promising but early. Lab and animal research suggests it may support the enzymes that break down alcohol and acetaldehyde and may have protective effects on the liver, while human data is still limited. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers in everyone, and it isn't a reason to drink more.

If you want to try DHM alongside sensible habits, options our readers use include [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), a straightforward budget pick, and [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which combines DHM with other ingredients. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much to take and when, and our [honest review of the DHM research](/never-hungover/does-dhm-work-honest-science-review-2025) covers what the studies do and don't show.

Either way, breakfast still matters. A supplement doesn't replace water, food, and sleep.

## The Bottom Line

- Eggs are a genuinely good hangover breakfast: gentle, filling, nutrient-dense, and helpful for steadying your energy.
- They contain cysteine, which your body uses to help clear acetaldehyde and to make glutathione. That link is real chemistry, but a normal serving provides far less than the doses tested in supplement studies.
- There is no good evidence from human trials that eating eggs makes a hangover shorter or milder on its own.
- Cook them gently, pair them with toast or fruit and plenty of fluids, and skip raw-egg "cures."
- If you can't keep fluids down, are confused or very drowsy, or have severe stomach pain or vomiting blood, get medical help.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Are eggs good for a hangover?**

Yes, as food. Eggs are gentle on an upset stomach, provide protein that helps steady your blood sugar, and contain cysteine, an amino acid involved in clearing acetaldehyde and making glutathione. There is no good evidence that eggs cure or shorten a hangover on their own, but they're one of the more sensible things to eat the morning after drinking.

**Why do eggs help with hangovers?**

Three reasons. They contain cysteine, which can bind acetaldehyde (a toxic by-product of alcohol) and is a building block of the liver antioxidant glutathione. They're mild and easy to eat when you feel nauseated. And their protein and fat, paired with toast or fruit, help even out your energy if your blood sugar is low after drinking.

**How much cysteine is in an egg?**

Based on USDA nutrient data, a large egg contains very roughly 130 to 150 mg of cysteine, so two eggs provide something like 250 to 300 mg. That's well below the 1,200 mg dose used in the small Finnish supplement trial on cysteine and hangovers, so eggs shouldn't be thought of as a substitute for that kind of dose.

**Is a bacon, egg, and cheese sandwich good for a hangover?**

It can make you feel better if your stomach handles it, because it combines protein, carbohydrate, fat, and salt. But very greasy food can worsen nausea or reflux for some people, and it doesn't "soak up" alcohol the next morning because the alcohol is already absorbed. If you're queasy, a lighter option like egg on toast is usually easier.

**What's the best way to cook eggs for a hangover?**

Soft scrambled or boiled eggs are the gentlest on an unsettled stomach. Poached eggs on toast add helpful carbohydrate. Brothy egg soups such as egg drop soup also add fluid and sodium. Avoid raw eggs because of the risk of food poisoning.

**Do raw eggs (a prairie oyster) cure a hangover?**

There's no good evidence that a raw egg drink works better than a cooked egg, and raw eggs can carry Salmonella, which causes food poisoning. Food safety agencies advise against eating raw or undercooked eggs, especially for pregnant people, older adults, young children, and people with weakened immune systems.

**Should I eat eggs before drinking or the morning after?**

Both can help in different ways. A meal with protein and fat before or while drinking slows how quickly alcohol reaches your bloodstream, which tends to matter more for how you feel the next day. The morning after, eggs are a gentle, nourishing breakfast that helps you recover, but they can't undo heavy drinking.

**When should I see a doctor for a hangover?**

Get medical help if someone can't keep fluids down for several hours, vomits blood, has severe stomach pain, is confused, very drowsy, or hard to wake, has a seizure, or has slow or irregular breathing. These can signal alcohol poisoning or severe dehydration. Shaking, sweating, or hallucinations after cutting back on regular heavy drinking can be signs of withdrawal and also need medical care.
